final_answer: Antibiotic resistance arises through the evolutionary mechanism of natural selection. When antibiotics are introduced to a bacterial population, they kill susceptible strains while allowing resistant strains to survive. These resistant bacteria reproduce and pass on their resistance traits to subsequent generations, leading to an increase in the proportion of resistant individuals within the population over time. This process is accelerated by overprescription of antibiotics, as excessive or inappropriate use exposes bacteria to selective pressure more frequently. This pressure eliminates sensitive strains and favors the proliferation of resistant ones, even in cases where antibiotics are unnecessary, such as treating viral infections. Overprescription also increases the likelihood of incomplete treatment regimens, which allows partially resistant bacteria to survive and further evolve. Thus, the misuse of antibiotics disrupts the balance of natural selection, favoring resistance and reducing the effectiveness of available treatments.
